content: 1. The IMPAACT P1066 study team investigated the pharmacokinetics, safety, and 48-week efficacy of oral raltegravir in children aged 2 to 18 years infected with HIV-1. The study provided critical data on the use of raltegravir in pediatric populations. (Clin Infect Dis. 2014;58(3):413–22). 2. Prendergast et al. emphasized the importance of evidence-based approaches to inform policymakers on the treatment of young children with HIV infection. Their work highlighted the need for tailored strategies to optimize outcomes in this vulnerable population. (PLoS Med. 2012;9(7):e1001273). 3. Penazzato et al. reviewed strategies for optimizing antiretroviral therapy in HIV-infected children under three years of age, providing insights into treatment regimens suitable for this age group. (Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2014;(5):CD004772). 4. Palumbo et al. examined the efficacy of antiretroviral treatment in children exposed to peripartum nevirapine, offering guidance on managing resistance and treatment outcomes. (N Engl J Med. 2010;363:1510–20). 5. Violari et al. compared nevirapine and ritonavir-boosted lopinavir in HIV-infected children, providing evidence to guide treatment decisions in pediatric HIV care. (N Engl J Med. 2012;366:2380–9). 6. Coovadia et al. conducted a randomized clinical trial in South Africa to evaluate efavirenz-based antiretroviral therapy in nevirapine-exposed HIV-infected children, demonstrating its efficacy and safety. (JAMA. 2015;314(17):1808–17). 7. Timité-Konan et al. explored the potential of efavirenz-based therapy to simplify lopinavir-based regimens initiated in HIV-1-infected children under two years of age in West Africa, as part of the MONOD trial. (7th International Workshop on HIV Pediatrics, 2015, Vancouver, Canada). 8. Kuhn et al. investigated drug resistance patterns in newly diagnosed HIV-infected children during an era of more effective antiretroviral prophylaxis, highlighting the challenges of resistance in pediatric populations. (AIDS. 2014;28(11):1673–8). 9. Chakanuka-Musanhu et al. reported on WHO HIV drug resistance surveillance in children under 18 months newly diagnosed with HIV in Zimbabwe, providing critical data for public health interventions. (7th IAS Conference on HIV Pathogenesis, Treatment, and Prevention, 2013, Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia). 10. Violari et al. analyzed the long-term virological and resistance outcomes of early ART initiation in infants, using data from the CHER trial after six years of follow-up. (11th International Congress on Drug Therapy in HIV Infection, 2012, Glasgow, UK). 11. Donegan et al. assessed the prevalence of darunavir-associated mutations in HIV-1-infected children in the UK, contributing to the understanding of resistance patterns in pediatric cohorts. (Antivir Ther. 2012;17:599–603). 12. Achan et al. evaluated the use of antiretroviral agents for malaria prevention in HIV-infected Ugandan children, providing insights into the dual management of HIV and malaria. (N Engl J Med. 2012;367:2110–18). 13. Musiime et al. studied the pharmacokinetics and acceptability of lopinavir/ritonavir formulations (minitab sprinkles, tablets, and syrups) in African HIV-infected children, offering practical guidance for treatment. (J Acquir Immune Defic Syndr. 2014;66(2):148–54). 14. Kekitiinwa et al. explored the acceptability of lopinavir/ritonavir minitabs, tablets, and syrups in HIV-infected children, emphasizing the importance of formulation preferences in pediatric care. (Accessed October 19, 2015). 15. Coovadia et al. investigated the reuse of nevirapine in HIV-infected children previously exposed to the drug, following viral suppression with protease inhibitor-based regimens. (JAMA. 2010;304:1082–90). 16. Kuhn et al. conducted a long-term follow-up study on switching nevirapine-exposed children to nevirapine-based treatment after initial suppression with protease inhibitors. (Lancet Infect Dis. 2012;12:521–30). 17. The FDA provided detailed information on the pharmacological properties and clinical use of Isentress (raltegravir), a key antiretroviral agent. (Accessed September 28, 2015). 18. Pillay et al. discussed the implications of HIV drug resistance on firstand second-line therapies in resource-limited settings, emphasizing the need for robust resistance monitoring. (Antivir Ther. 2013;18(6):831–6). 19. The Pediatric ARV Drug Optimization 2 meeting report outlined strategies for improving antiretroviral therapy in children, focusing on drug formulations and dosing. (Accessed October 19, 2015). 20. Ford et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on the causes of hospital admissions among people living with HIV worldwide, identifying key areas for intervention. (Lancet HIV. 2015;2:e438–44). 21. Rabie et al. evaluated the pharmacokinetics of lopinavir/ritonavir in the presence of rifampicin in HIV-infected children, providing evidence for dose adjustments in co-treatment scenarios. (7th International Workshop on HIV Pediatrics, 2015, Vancouver, Canada). 22. The Panel on Antiretroviral Therapy and Medical Management of HIV-Infected Children published guidelines for the use of antiretroviral agents in pediatric HIV infection, offering comprehensive recommendations. (Accessed October 19, 2015). 23. van Dijk et al. assessed the effectiveness of efavirenz-based regimens in young HIV-infected children treated for tuberculosis, highlighting its utility in resource-limited settings. (PLoS One. 2013;8:e55111). 24. Drake et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on the risk of mother-to-child HIV transmission during pregnancy and postpartum, emphasizing the importance of incident HIV prevention. (PLoS Med. 2014;11(2):e1001608). 25. Moodley et al. examined the impact of incident HIV infection in pregnant and lactating women on mother-to-child transmission rates in South Africa, providing critical epidemiological data. (J Infect Dis. 2011;203:1231–4). 26. Humphrey et al. studied postnatal seroconversion and its impact on mother-to-child HIV transmission in Zimbabwean women, offering insights into prevention strategies. (BMJ. 2010;341:c6580). 27. Beste et al. reviewed optimal antiretroviral prophylaxis regimens for infants at high risk of acquiring HIV, contributing to the development of evidence-based guidelines. (NICHD HPTN 040/PACTG 1043 Protocol Team). 28. Coovadia et al. evaluated the efficacy and safety of extended nevirapine regimens in breastfeeding infants of HIV-infected mothers, as part of the HPTN 046 trial. (Lancet. 2012;379(9812):221–8). 29. Chiappini et al. analyzed the use of combination neonatal prophylaxis for preventing mother-to-child HIV transmission in high-risk infants in Europe. (AIDS. 2013;27:991–1000). 30. Lallemant et al. discussed the intensification of antiretroviral therapy to prevent intrapartum HIV transmission in late-presenting mothers. (8th IAS Conference on HIV Pathogenesis, Treatment, and Prevention, 2015, Vancouver, Canada). 31. Irvine explored values and preferences regarding the duration of infant prophylaxis, contributing to the development of patient-centered care guidelines. (Web Supplement C). 32. Schneider et al. investigated the presence of efavirenz in breast milk and its implications for maternal and neonatal plasma levels, providing data on drug safety during breastfeeding. (J Acquir Immune Defic Syndr. 2008;48:450–4). 33. Harrigan et al. examined the predictive value of intermittent viremia in patients on combination HIV therapy, offering insights into treatment monitoring. (JAMA. 2001;286:171–9). 34. Rutherford et al. reviewed the performance of WHO immunologic and clinical criteria for predicting virologic failure in adults and children on antiretroviral therapy. (AIDS. 2014;28:161–9). 35. Koller et al. developed and validated risk charts to guide targeted HIV-1 viral load monitoring in resource-limited settings, improving ART management. (J Acquir Immune Defic Syndr. 2015;70(3):e110–19). 36. Yotebieng et al. established ageand sex-specific weight gain norms for monitoring ART in children in lowand middle-income countries. (AIDS. 2015;29(1):101–9). 37. Chow et al. demonstrated that routine CD4 cell count monitoring rarely influences clinical decision-making in virologically suppressed HIV-infected patients. (HIV Med. 2015;16(3):196–200). 38. Hyle et al. highlighted potential cost savings from reduced CD4 monitoring in stable HIV patients on ART. (JAMA Intern Med. 2013;173(18):1746–8). 39. Duncan et al. questioned the utility of CD4+ monitoring in HIV-1 patients with counts above 350 cells/µl on suppressive ART. (AIDS. 2014;28(17):2638–9). 40. Davies et al. proposed reducing CD4 monitoring in children on ART with virologic suppression, emphasizing resource optimization. (Pediatr Infect Dis J. 2015;34:1361–4). 41. Cooper et al. reviewed combination antiretroviral strategies for pregnant HIV-1-infected women to prevent perinatal transmission. (J Acquir Immune Defic Syndr. 2002;29(5):484–94). 42. Townsend et al. reported on the decline in mother-to-child HIV transmission rates with earlier ART initiation from 2000 to 2011. (AIDS. 2014;28(7):1049–57). 43. Vojnov demonstrated the feasibility of using dried blood spot samples for HIV-1 viral load testing with current technologies. (Web Supplement B). 44. Phillips et al. advocated for sustainable HIV treatment in Africa through viral-load-informed differentiated care. (Nature. 528:S66–S76). 45. Harrigan et al. identified predictors of HIV drug-resistance mutations in a large cohort initiating triple antiretroviral therapy. (J Infect Dis. 2005;191(3):339–47).
